#8390. Adventure Links of the Week

When we’re not outdoors, we get our adventure fix by exploring social media and the web. Here are some of the best adventure links we’ve discovered this week.

Yosemite Visitors Join Forces To Perform Extraordinary Rescue on Half Dome: When a Polish hiker slipped while descending the cables on Yosemite’s Half Dome, she slid down the steep granite face and was left clinging to the rock. Her fiancé then lost his footing while trying to reach her.

A group of strangers came together to rescue the pair. Using ropes, slings, carabiners, and climbing harnesses, the group formed a human chain to reach both stranded hikers and pull them to safety.

The Electric Arms Race Has Gone Too Far: Tim Shuff questions the growing use of electric motors in outdoor adventure. He argues that the speed and convenience they create undermine traditionally self-propelled activities like paddling and cycling. Today, you can even buy battery-powered SUPs.

While recognizing that electric assistance can make outdoor sports more accessible, he thinks that its wider use will change wilderness areas, reshape trails, and create pressure to build increasingly powerful equipment.

Jan Spicka descends from Huascarán Sur. Photo: Matej Zak

A Czech Alpinist Describes How He Survived a Nightmare on Peru’s Highest Mountain: Climbing Peru’s Huascarán Sur turned into a tragedy for a group of five friends last July. Czech alpinist Jan Spicka describes how he and partner Matej Zak reached the 6,768m summit before he plunged into a hidden crevasse on the descent.

Matej’s quick reactions saved his life, but their three friends, Saul Mendoza, Chicho Ugarte, and Arti Salas, disappeared while attempting to descend by a different route. With no official mountain rescue in Peru, friends and volunteers pitched in. After 24 hours in the freezing conditions, they knew it was unlikely they would see their friends again. GPS tracks and later searches suggest they had fallen through a collapsing snow bridge.

He Felt Stuck in New York. So He Started Walking to California: Feeling trapped by unemployment and a lack of opportunities in New York, 29-year-old Chantz Rivera began walking across America. He set off with a tent, sleeping bag, and some supplies in a shopping cart. Over 149 days, he walked to California, pushing his cart 32 to 40km a day along highways and through small towns, documenting his progress for his growing number of online followers.

This Mountain Race Makes Runners Carry 60kg of Beer and Supplies Uphill: Slovakia’s annual Sherpa Rallye is one of the world’s unique mountain races. Competitors have to haul heavy loads of supplies up a 5.7km rocky trail to a remote hut in the High Tatras, nearly 2,000m above sea level.

Men carry 60kg, including a 30-liter keg of beer, while women carry 20kg, with the loads secured to wooden frames. The race was started in 1985 by mountain porter Viktor Beranek. The event brings together the region’s nosiči (traditional mountain porters) and also helps stock the remote hut ahead of winter.

A Hiker Slid Hundreds of Meters Down Mount Timpanogos: A female hiker was seriously injured after slipping off the trail near the summit of Mount Timpanogos in Utah. She slid several hundred feet down the steep mountainside before landing on a narrow cliff ledge. Newly released helicopter footage shows her being hoisted to safety. She was taken to hospital and is reportedly recovering.

We Need to Move Past the ‘Shut Up and Die Like a Man’ Mentality in the Mountains: Climber and paraglider Will Gadd reflects on the psychological impact of mountain accidents. Climbing culture often glorifies the dangers people face in the mountains while discouraging them from admitting they are struggling.

Gadd discusses the deaths of two close friends and challenges the underlying expectation that climbers should simply suck it up and carry on. After decades in the mountains, he has seen that the consequences of an accident extend far beyond the immediate incident, affecting survivors and their families and friends for years.

Two Hikers Dead in Bear Attack in British Columbia: Two hikers, identified as 48-year-old Jennifer Balcarras and her 20-year-old daughter Selah Reed, have died in a suspected grizzly attack near the Snooka West Trail in Bella Coola, British Columbia. Their bodies were found during a search after the pair were reported missing by their family.

This comes just a year after a separate grizzly attack in the same area severely injured four people, including three children. The trail remains closed as authorities continue their investigation.

Rebecca McPhee is a freelance writer for ExplorersWeb.

Based in the UK Rebecca is a science teacher and volunteers for a number of marine charities. She enjoys open water swimming, hiking, diving, and traveling.

#8389. Oasis in the 100-mile (Day 164)

Dreamcatcher and I had an earlier start today, Small Bites is taking his time this morning, he’ll catch up to us later. We hiked into quite a scene today. There is a full wreckage of an airplane crash here! We read about the story and all survived, seeing the remnants of the plane however, I truly wonder how.

My trail name is Hungry, but this might be the first time I actually am truly getting hungry on the trail. Dreamcatcher needs more food too. We packed a little bit too efficiently I guess. The 100-mile isn’t the best place to do that, since there are no resupply points for days.

We noticed something on our maps that neither of us had heard of before: an AMC hut in the 100-mile wilderness?! It’s a little blue blaze off trail. Considering our situation regarding food, we might as well check it out. Maybe they have something. Small Bites caught up to us again.

Maybe doesn’t look like it, but this was a godsend

We can’t sit here forever though, so we continued and forded a river and hiked on some nice trail, not the usual rocky and rooty stuff.

#8385. Antarctica 2026-2027: Expedition Roundup

Here are the Antarctic expeditions for 2026-27. There will be more, as a few still scramble to raise the money or choose to keep their plans to themselves until the last minute. Because of the long charter flights, an expedition to Antarctica, even a “tourist” Last Degree trip, costs close to $100,000 — more, if you want to do something unusual. These are the journeys announced so far. Skiers hit the ice later this month.

Hercules Inlet is the common starting point for South Pole skiers. Skiers need to travel around 1,130km, averaging around 20km per day.

Brit Nathan Lumb originally planned a fully unsupported round-trip to the South Pole but scaled back due to “expedition logistics and funding realities.” He will now ski solo and unsupported from Hercules Inlet to the South Pole. Lumb previously completed a crossing of Norway’s Finnmarksvidda with guiding company Ousland Colliard.

Indian Neeraj Choudhary also trained with Ousland Colliard, crossing the Greenland Ice Sheet in 2024. He hopes to become the second Indian to ski solo and unsupported to the South Pole, following Satish Gogineni, who became the first in 2024-2025.

Satish Gogineni at the South Pole in 2025. Photo: Satish Gogineni

American Lucas Czarnecki will also ski solo and unsupported and claims he will livestream every moment of his journey: “What sets South Signal [his expedition name] apart from other polar expeditions is my commitment to bringing you along for every moment of this extreme adventure. Each day, I will be live-streaming my experience directly from the ice, sharing the raw reality of life on the polar plateau.”

Another American, Meghan Buchanan, will also tackle the route. She plans to start early, leaving for Antarctica on November 12.

Finally, German Dirk Langer will also attempt the route unsupported.

A Berkner Island start means a few extra kilometers, with skiers required to cover around 1,400km to the South Pole.

Max Worsley of the UK and Martin Nesse of Norway also plan to start in early November, but from the edge of Berkner Island. Max is the son of Henry Worsley, who died following an Antarctic expedition in 2015-2016. Max intends to follow much of his father’s final route.

At least two expeditions will begin at the Messner start, 911km from the South Pole. James Garnett of the UK and Norwegian Marius Rehn will each ski solo and unsupported.

Satish Gogineni will be back in Antarctica this year, hoping to build upon his Hercules Inlet experience. Gogineni’s 2026 plan is more ambitious: a solo, 2,000km journey from the outer edge of the Filchner–Ronne Ice Shelf to the inner edge of the Ross Ice Shelf via the South Pole. Gogineni is billing this as a “world-first human achievement” and the “longest solo traverse ever completed on the Antarctic continent.”

If successful, his route would indeed be longer than the truncated crossings of Colin O’Brady and Lou Rudd in 2018. However, his distance would still be well short of Borge Ousland’s 1997 expedition. Ousland became the first person to cross Antarctica solo and unsupported, though he occasionally used a rudimentary handheld kite known as a ski sail. Ousland skied for 65 days and covered 2,845km. At the time, sails were not considered “support.”

Last year, O’Brady tried a significantly longer expedition than his 2018 effort, attempting to ski from the edge of the Ross Ice Shelf to the tip of Berkner Island on the edge of the Ronne Ice Shelf, a total distance of over 2,800km. He eventually ended his crossing attempt after 100 days, with roughly 40% of his total distance remaining.

A map by PECS (the Polar Expeditions Classification Scheme) showing previous solo Antarctic crossing routes. Photo: PECS

Gogineni’s main challenge might be the weight of his sled. With so much weight spread over two sleds, O’Brady was forced to double carry in soft snow on the Ross Ice Shelf last year. A double carry involved shuttling half of his gear forward, then returning to pick up the rest. This meant he had to cover 15km for every 5km of progress. Gogineni says his sled will weigh 181kg.

Mardi Philips, Ida Olsson, and Nia Owens are calling themselves the Antarctic Valkyries and aim to become the “first all-female team to reach the South Pole of Inaccessibility.” They will start at Thorshammer Station (a spot near the Russian Novolazarevskaya Station in Queen Maud Land) and plan to kite-ski 2,500km, first aiming for the Pole of Inaccessibility (the middle of the Antarctic continent), and then continuing to their finish point at the South Pole.

The Antarctic Valkyries proposed route. Photo: Antarctic Valkyries

A Spanish scientific expedition will cross Antarctica by a new route in a unique wind-powered vehicle.

Part of the wind-sled involves a series of tents. Photo: La Vanguardia

Their “wind-sled ” is 15m long and consists of four modules. It is propelled using 20 kites of various sizes. The largest kite measures 150m² and the smallest 5m². The four-man team plans a 3,400km, 85-day journey from near Novolazarevskaya Station to the Italian research station Concordia, known as Dome C, on the Antarctic Plateau.

The wind-sled team’s proposed route. The green return route is planned for a future expedition. Photo: La Vanguardia

Meanwhile, three Argentine kayakers are preparing to paddle roughly 900km along the western coast of the Antarctic Peninsula, from Argentina’s Esperanza Base to San Martín Base. Diego Linares, Juan Tomaselli, and Javier Siede will start their journey in January and plan to spend 30 to 40 days on the water.

Martin Walsh is a writer and editor for ExplorersWeb.

Martin spent most of the last 20 years backpacking the world on a shoestring budget. Whether it was hitchhiking through Syria, getting strangled in Kyrgyzstan, touring Cambodia’s medical facilities with an exceedingly painful giant venomous centipede bite, chewing khat in Ethiopia, or narrowly avoiding various toilet-related accidents in rural China, so far, Martin has just about survived his decision-making.

Based in Da Lat, Vietnam, Martin can be found in the jungle trying to avoid leeches while chasing monkeys.

#8381. A Risky Summit Push on Everest

It’s now or never for the Russian team on the West Ridge of Everest. Andrey Vasiliev, Sergey Kondrashkin, and Vitaly Shipilov have set off for the summit without oxygen, hoping the weather will hold. They are completely alone on the mountain, and the push is full of risk.

Everest is still loaded with fresh snow after two cyclones, and there are only three of them to break trail and find the best route above 7,500m. That was their highest point during their earlier venture in October.  In addition, the wind may rise dramatically on Thursday, Vitor Baia, a Portuguese high-altitude meteorologist, told ExplorersWeb.

“It looks like we have a weather window of about a week, followed by a significant intensification of the wind,” leader Andrei Vasiliev told Anna Piunova of Mountain Club.

The question is exactly when the wind will increase, and whether the climbers will have enough time to summit and descend to a safer altitude.

“They have three days of weak wind, until Wednesday [November 11], but then the wind will increase sharply,” said Baia.

He says the best summit day will be Tuesday, with clear skies and weak winds. “Then they could use Wednesday to descend,” he added. “[That day will have] some clouds but still acceptable wind speeds.”

The situation will worsen remarkably on Thursday, when the wind will shift from the west to the northwest and increase dramatically to 50 kph at 8,000m and 60kph at the summit.

In addition, avalanche hazards are still high due to the large amounts of snow after the latest storm two weeks ago. Finally, as winter approaches, it’s getting colder every day, the climbers reported.

After their first trip up ended in a tactical retreat as the cyclone hit, they retreated to Kathmandu to recover from some health issues. Now they are fit again and ready for a second try. They returned to Base Camp last Thursday. Not surprisingly, they found it covered in a thick new layer of snow. Breaking trail, they sank at some points up to their waists, Vasiliev reported.

“Our high-altitude boots were in a cache two hours ahead of us, so we used duct tape to seal our pant cuffs to our trekking boots, trying to keep the snow out,” Kondrashkin reported. They eventually reached the cache and continued up in an exhausting 14-hour-long effort to a second cache (their Camp 1), where they had left their tent and sleeping bags.

They were near an avalanche-prone area and several snow slides swept nearby, prompting them to wait a day before continuing. Meanwhile, Shipilov showed signs of food poisoning. Kodrashkin recalls that Saturday morning started with the following conversation:

“Vitalya, how are you feeling? Are we heading up?”

That answer needs some clarification. A professional like Vitaly Viktorovich [Shipilov] really only has two modes: “We’re going” and “I’m dying.”

In fact, Shipilov had a fever and acute pain in the lower back, so the team headed down to their base in Lobuche. As this was going on, the snow had time to sluff off from the previously avalanche-prone area.

After just one night of rest, Vasiliev confirmed they were going up again. If all went according to plan, they will spend tonight back in their tent above the Lho La. Unfortunately, the climbers have not shared their tracker showing their current location and progress. On their previous trip up, they reached some 7,500m on Everest’s West Shoulder, near the beginning of the West Ridge and the potential detour to the Hornbein Couloir.

Everest’s North Face from the base of the West Ridge. Photo: Sergey Kondrashkin

#8379. The Hidden Financial Stress of Thru-Hiking

For better or worse, I was born with the fiscal sensibilities of a Depression-era grandmother. This can be both an asset and a liability for thru-hiking. Back in the day, my frugal spending habits made it easier to save enough money to comfortably thru-hike the Appalachian Trail, but they were also an unexpected handicap once I was actually on trail.

People rarely talk about how psychologically challenging it can be to live with the stress of spending without earning for the six-ish months that a long thru-hike usually takes, and I definitely wasn’t prepared for it. Money stress comes in many forms, but most people experience it one way or another — and that struggle can follow you out onto the trail.

In today’s challenging economy, it’s more important than ever for aspiring thru-hikers to consider not just whether they can afford to hike, but how they’ll cope with the psychological stress of watching their savings dwindle with each passing mile. It’s easy to take fiscal responsibility too far and get caught up in an unhelpful scarcity mindset. Don’t let that be you.

Hiking is hard. Don’t make it harder by beating yourself up for literally no reason.

Thru-hikers often talk about how easy it is to spend way too much money on zero days. For me, spending money in town was one of the hardest things about the trail. I’m not saying I didn’t spend — the lure of a soft bed and a hiker-sized restaurant meal was usually enough to overpower my frugality — but I agonized over every purchase in every single town. There were times when I even felt so guilty about the spending that I considered ending my hike early.

It wasn’t just that I was spending money without replacing it; it was that I wasn’t doing anything about it. I wasn’t applying for jobs or upskilling or preparing myself to reenter the job market. I was just existing in the woods day in and day out, being thoroughly unproductive, with no particular plan for after the trail. This was apparently too much for my little capitalist brain to handle.

This mindset would have been more reasonable if lack of funds was a serious threat to my thru-hiking goals. But I had been fortunate enough to save enough money that I didn’t need to worry about running out mid-hike. I spent half my time worrying about running out of money for literally no reason.

Me mentally berating myself for overspending on name-brand peanut butter, probably.

What is the solution? Should I have saved even more money ahead of time? Of course that wouldn’t hurt, but such is the nature of anxiety that I doubt it would have stopped me from stressing. Should I have taken out a Coursera subscription and spent my evenings in camp learning how to code, or treated every impromptu hiker gathering like a networking event?

Obviously not. In reality, there’s usually no easy solution to the assorted neuroses that play out in our heads. In my case, it was just a matter of learning to live with the uncertainty of not having an income or a guaranteed path back into paid work after the hike. I was afraid of not having enough or of being unable to find another job, and I just had to face that fear.

The AT forced me to confront my own limiting beliefs around money. In the years since that first thru-hike, I’ve gotten a little more relaxed about spending money on things I know I can afford without feeling guilty about it. I haven’t abandoned my frugal tendencies, but they don’t need to dictate every decision I make. I credit the trail for that growth.

“I wonder if I can get another 200 miles out of these shoes before I replace them. I wonder if I should get on a cheaper insurance plan next year. Do I have enough money to buy name-brand peanut butter in the next town? Should I get a different credit card? Should I go stoveless to save on fuel? “

I’ve written a few articles over the years about my peculiar hiking-related neuroses. As always, I want to clarify in the midst of all this doom and gloom that thru-hiking was and is one of the great joys of my life, despite my assorted pathologies and the mistakes I’ve made along the way.

Every thru-hiker will face struggles both external and internal; learning to deal with and overcome them is part of the experience, and this is just one more example. As always, do everything you can to prepare for your thru-hike, accept that you can’t plan for everything, and then enjoy the journey, hardships and all.

#8375. Winners of the Banff Mountain Film Festival Announced

The annual Banff Centre Mountain Festival gathers mountain luminaries from across the world at the Banff Centre for Arts and Creativity in Alberta. There, a celebration of mountain culture recognizes the best outdoor films and books of the past year. The climax of the festival took place this past weekend, and the winners of the 51st annual Banff Mountain Film Competition have now been announced.

The Grand Prize went to Listen, directed by Taliesin Black-Brown. In this short documentary, sound engineer Hank Lentfer records the sounds of nature around his Alaska home, while caring for his mother with dementia. As Lentfer documents the degradation of the natural world, we witness the slow loss of his mother. Drawing together these two threads, the film explores connection despite, and through, loss, using sound.

Rose Bush, an Oscar Award-winning director of photography serving on the competition’s jury, called Listen “a film that engages human-caused environmental devastation — the existential dilemma of our time — at its nucleus with overwhelming love and hope.”

The film also won the Grand Jury Prize at the Tribeca Film Festival.

In addition to a grand prize, the festival honors films in several categories. The winning film in the Adventure category was The Navigator, a feature-length work from director Jordan Manley. The film follows Nainoa Thompson, who was the first Native Hawaiian in six centuries to make the journey from Hawaii to Tahiti in a traditional voyaging canoe. Now, almost five decades later, Thompson and his crew make the journey again, using only traditional navigation techniques.

The best film in the Mountain Culture category was Land of Canaan, produced and directed by Maggie Lemere. Lemere’s film follows a group of Palestinian olive farmers, who work to protect their ancient olive groves amid the destruction by Israel. The film “illuminated the vital relationship of courage, vision, hope, and traditional ecological knowledge,” juror Rose Bush said, “in service of the essential value of sovereignty via mountain culture.”

In the Environment category, director James Dawson’s winning comedic documentary Derek vs Derek follows two Devon farmers, both named Derek. One Derek is an ardent dairy farmer while his environmentalist neighbor begins rewilding his land. A feud naturally ensues.

The Arc’teryx-sponsored Best Climbing Film was Zindabad, directed by Tom Fish. Fish follows Pakistani climber Mueez Ud Din into the Karakoram, alongside his uncle Javed Ali and French climber Mathieu Maynadier. Ud Din explores a remote, unknown glacier system, while the film examines what it means to be a Pakistani climber among peaks long claimed by international outsiders.

Directed by Alexis Berg, the Mountain Sports winner, Roots, follows trail runner Ruth Croft as she examines her future as an elite ultra-trail runner after an injury. Roots is “about an inner journey of healing and acceptance, rooted in the essential joy of running outdoors,” explained juror David Arnaud.

The Snow Sports winner centers on American skier Jessie Diggins. Diggins is the most decorated American cross-country skier ever, but Threshold, directed by Torsten Brinkema, reveals the deep personal struggles behind that success. Juror Beki Henderson noted that “the jury particularly commends Jessie Diggins for her extraordinary courage and honesty in sharing her story.”

There were more mountain films this year than you can even imagine. With 610 film submissions and 83 finalists, it’s no wonder that there are still more category winners.

Best short film winner Hello, Beautiful follows climber Alannah Yip as she struggles with identity, training for the Olympics while enduring medical hair loss. Director Darcy Hennessey created a film which “reminds us that personal transformation does not always come from pushing harder,” juror Kerry Stauffer explained.

For best feature film, the competition announced Ceremony, directed and produced by Banchi Hanuse. The film tells the story of the disappearance of the ooligan, a small fish, from British Columbia’s Bella Coola River. Jurors praised the film’s use of watercolor animation, personal stories, and community broadcasts to explore the importance of a seemingly unimportant little fish.

Director Marco Tribelhorn’s 75 seconds won the Creative Excellence Award. The film documents free-skier Jacob Wester’s 75-second-long battle for survival while trapped in an avalanche.

“A compelling visual treatment brings to life an experience that is impossible to imagine,” said Kerry Stauffer.

Last but not least, the Audience Choice Award went to Only Music // Snake River. Director Justin Fountain’s documentary follows a band that ditches the tour bus for a journey down the Snake River, seeking connection with strangers.

Tickets for the international film festival are now available. We have also covered the recently announced Banff Mountain Book Award winners.

Lou Bodenhemier holds an MA in History from the University of Limerick and a BA in Creative Writing from the University of Arizona. #8373. ‘Not Your Daddy’s 22.’ This Is The Best 22 Creedmoor Ammo for Deer Hunting

Published Nov 9, 2026 9:00 AM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

The latest for gun hunters and competitive shooters.

New cartridges like the 22 Creedmoor and 22 ARC have been developed alongside the modern practice of leveraging heavy-for-caliber bullets into better downrange performance and, as it turns out, the 22 Creedmoor is a stone-cold deer killer. There are still relatively limited factory ammo options compared to legacy cartridges, and if you’re looking for the best 22 Creedmoor ammo for deer specifically, there are a couple of important considerations. Here’s a look at five of the solid options we have tested for accuracy and velocity, using the bullets that have killed deer and other big game with. Being that Hornady brought the cartridge to SAAMI for standardization, they have the widest variety of factory ammo, but there are other good options too.

People get a lot of big feelings when you broach the subject of shooting big-game animals with .22-caliber rifles, so it’s important to talk about what we mean, and what we don’t. There have undoubtedly been thousands of deer killed with various varmint bullets and .22 rimfire cartridges with a wide variety of results.

That’s not what we’re talking about here.

As numerous insightful old timers discovered by loading cartridges like the .220 Swift, .22/250 Remington, and .223 Remington with more purposeful bullets — sometimes requiring tighter twist barrels — .22-caliber centerfires kill deer very effectively.

The 22 Creedmoor, with the same bullets and barrel length, will leave even the great Swift in the dust, and it’s specifically designed to work best with modern, long, high-BC bullets that maintain their speed and terminal effectiveness hundreds of yards beyond what traditional 40- to 60-grain .224 bullets could. These bullets are perfectly capable of delivering decisive penetration and trauma on any reasonable shot at a deer.

There are a couple important things to consider when picking the best 22 Creedmoor ammo for deer. First is bullet weight and construction. There isn’t currently a plethora of 22 Creed factory ammo on the market, but it’s wise to avoid the varmint-specific loads. Many varmint bullets are designed specifically to be fragile. At some of the velocities you’ll see from these 22 Creed varmint loads, the volatile bullets can sometimes not penetrate well.

An example of this is Hornady’s 62-grain ELD-VT, launched with the 22 ARC in mind. According to Hornady their shooters, after killing hundreds of coyotes, noticed that they saw a higher percentage of them running after being hit when the 62-grain ELD-VT was used in the 22 CM than when it was launched slightly slower out of the ARC. The problem was remedied with a slightly heavier 69-grain slug. Deer aren’t exceptionally big or dense animals, and there are other ammo options that will work well.

The other consideration isn’t as straightforward, and is one significant drawback of the 22 Creedmoor. Its standardized twist rate of 1:8 accommodates those more fragile bullets at high velocities while generally stabilizing the heavy-for-caliber 80-plus-grain bullets — but not always. At low elevations and in cold weather, your bullets can lose stability, and your accuracy can go to hell completely.

I first noticed this while shooting at about 28 degrees Fahrenheit and 1,000 feet of elevation. This barrel consistently printed 20-shot samples under an inch with the 80-grain ELD-X, but, beyond 600 yards, my bullets were dropping way more than they had been doing a few days prior when it was warmer. Later, at 0 degrees Fahrenheit, groups at 100 yards opened up to nearly 6 inches with the same bullets. I’ve documented this instability, which varies from barrel to barrel, in several guns now.

The takeaway is that if you are going to be hunting late season at low elevation in cold temperatures, either choose a bullet that will work reliably in a 1:8-twist barrel, or at least test your rifle and ammo in those conditions before hunting.

The 80-grain ELD-X is one of the best all-around .22-cal performers for larger game. This bullet follows the same general design as other ELD-X bullets, featuring a lead core and mechanical internal locking ring to control expansion. It has Hornady’s heat shield tip with DRVT for more consistent drag. This is one of the most efficient hunting-specific .22-cal bullets there is, with a BC that allows it to stay above 2,000 fps for over 600 yards in the 22 Creedmoor. The most unique characteristic to this bullet — compared to the ELD-X in other calibers — is that it has a proportionally thicker jacket. This was to ensure controlled expansion even at velocities over 3,000 fps.

This bullet has proven to penetrate well and do a lot of damage. I shot a whitetail buck with the 80-grain ELD-X loaded in a .223, which would have been the equivalent of about a 450-yard shot from the 22 Creed. It hit the buck, which was quartering to, through the front shoulder and exited halfway back the ribs on the opposite side. I’ve also executed a similar shot on a huge black bear from about 15 yards with a 22 ARC — leaving the bullet under the offside hide after about 18 inches of penetration.

This is an all-around performer in the 22 Creedmoor, but is more optimal in a 1:7-twist barrel. If you’re planning on using it in cold weather, you should test it beforehand.

Many hunters will intentionally steer clear of match ammunition and Hornady does not recommend this ammo for deer hunting. Sometimes folks try stuff without asking permission, however, and it ends up working pretty damned well. Now, seeing how well the 80-grain ELD-X works, I’m not compelled to choose the nearly identical ELD-M bullet over it. They have the same BC and often have nearly the same point of impact and velocity. But this load has crushed a lot of bucks and is a favorite of Derrick Ratliff of Horizon Firearms and one of the big players in bringing the 22 Creed to the commercial market.

The ELD-M bullet will generally be more fragile than the ELD-X, and it creates even more violent wound cavities. This doesn’t mean it explodes on shoulders and won’t penetrate — that’s not the case. But when seeing the holes it puts through deer, you may want to tone it down. There’s no harm if you choose a more rigidly constructed bullet, and you should always be thoughtful about the shots you do take by keeping your bullet construction in mind. Still, this ammo is out there killing bucks with authority.

If you need or want a monolithic copper bullet, this will likely be the only factory option you can find. It uses a 65-grain CX bullet, which is a comfortable 1:8-twist bullet. In testing, Hornady found the 70-grain CX — made for the 1:7-twist 22 ARC — doesn’t stabilize well. I was able to shoot a pronghorn with this bullet, handloaded for an 18-inch 22 Creedmoor, before factory ammo was available. The bullet passed through both shoulders and the buck was dead before he hit the ground.

If you’re a fan of shoulder-shooting deer, this is a bullet you will be very happy with. The CX is designed for high weight retention and won’t produce a wound as violent as the ELD-X or ELD-M, but it is a penetrating son-of-a-gun. The 65-grain CX has a lower BC than the 80-grain lead-core bullets, but has enough velocity to help it maintain a similar effective range. For most deer hunters choosing a 22 Creed, you’ll be hunting at distances where that lower BC won’t come into play.

We’ve been big fans of the Federal Fusion line for deer ammo because it’s affordable, shoots well, and delivers great terminal performance. Federal just announced this 22 Creedmoor deer ammo, but I saw the press release a few days after buying some in a local store, so it should be available for rifle seasons. This is probably the most affordable 22 Creed ammo that’s deer-appropriate, and it features the same plated jacket as other Fusion bullets.

I’ve gone through a couple boxes of this and the ammo shot pretty well. It averaged 3,100 fps from a 22-inch barrel, which would put it around 125 fps slower than box velocity of 3,300 fps in a 24-inch barrel. Velocities can vary depending on several factors, but it does track with a lot of factory 22 CM ammo in the 70-80-grain range which ranges from 3,050 to 3,200 fps from 20-inch barrels — the most common contemporary barrel length.

If maximizing efficiency is important to you, there are better bullets, but this should work comfortably at any temperature in a standard 1:8 twist barrel, and will deliver great performance for the needs of most deer hunters.

Another excellent option for deer would be Nosler’s 70-grain AccuBond offering. This is more of a legacy bullet — made for 1:9- or 1:8-twist barrels — that’s also loaded in .223, rather than one of the more optimized 22 Creedmoor options. I would love to see Nosler come out with a heavier, more efficient option that leverages the Creed’s case and chamber design and load this to a bit more competitive speeds. Still, this is a deadly and effective bullet at normal deer-hunting distances, and would be a good choice.

Modern bullets are what really make the 22 Creedmoor shine as a deer cartridge. We have options that are more efficient with more predictable performance than ever. If you want to hunt deer with a 22 Creedmoor, pick ammo that will fit how and where you hunt.

Read Next: Best Ammo for Deer Hunting, Tested for Accuracy

Most people won’t have to worry about bullet stability with factory ammo, but it’s something you need to pay attention to at low elevation in temperatures below freezing. As with any hunting rifle and ammo, the most important factor is you. Pick a rifle and ammo you like and get out there and practice.

#8370. A 3,300Km Walk Across Japan in Winter

Japanese publisher Katsunari Tanaka has set himself the challenge of hauling a handcart 3,345km from Japan’s northernmost tip to the southern edge of Okinawa in winter.

Tanaka, 49, set off from Cape Sōya in Hokkaido on October 7 and is heading south to Cape Hedo in Okinawa. He hopes to complete the traverse in 100 days over five months. As he will have to contend with some challenging winter conditions along the way, he has described it as “playing chase with winter.”

Rather than carrying everything on his back, he is pulling a handcart that weighs around 100kg. He also has a support team with a vehicle in case of emergencies. At some points, different members of his team have walked with him for a day or so. His daily target is around 35km, with rest days and organized stops built into the schedule.

The first few weeks have already brought strong headwinds, rain, and some steep climbs, making progress difficult at times. Temperatures have dropped close to freezing. At the end of October, he crossed a mountain pass between Yoichi and Iwanai. There, headwinds stirred up the gravel as he walked. Then the snow began. In the end, he took refuge with his support team until the weather improved.

Despite the conditions, Tanaka reached Hakodate Harbor on November 3, having covered 621km across Hokkaido. From Hakodate, he is crossing the Tsugaru Strait by ferry to Aomori, then will continue south along the Sanriku coast to Sendai.

From there, he follows the Pacific coast through Fukushima to Tokyo before joining the Tokaido route toward Osaka before heading west to Kyushu. A second ferry crossing brings him to Okinawa, where he will walk to his final destination, Cape Hedo.

Along a road in Hokkaido. Photo: Katsunari Tanaka/Instagram

This is not Tanaka’s first experience of traveling Japan with a handcart. Around a decade ago, he spent three years visiting all 47 prefectures, selling books directly to people he met along the way. Loading his publications onto a cart, he covered the country between 2013 and 2016, eventually selling 13,477 books. At the time, many people questioned what he was doing and whether books could really be sold on the street. But he says the experience shaped his approach to business and his belief in the power of personal connections.

Tanaka insists that he is not an adventurer. Instead, he is traveling the country as a “merchant.” This time, he is making the journey to support his mentor, Arthur Hollands, a Japanese evangelist known for undertaking lengthy walks while carrying a large wooden cross. Along the route, Tanaka plans to stop at 11 locations to give lectures. He welcomes people to join him for sections of the walk.

Rebecca McPhee is a freelance writer for ExplorersWeb.

Rebecca has been writing about open water sports, adventure travel, and marine science for three years. Prior to that, Rebecca worked as an Editorial Assistant at Taylor and Francis, and a Wildlife Officer for ORCA.

Based in the UK Rebecca is a science teacher and volunteers for a number of marine charities. She enjoys open water swimming, hiking, diving, and traveling.

#8368. ‘It’s a Different Race of Deer Up There.’ A High-Country Mule Deer Hunt for the Ages

Published Nov 9, 2026 11:00 AM EST

Get everything from whitetail news and opinion pieces, to advanced hunting tactics and cutting-edge gear reviews.

“IT’S A DIFFERENT race of deer up there,” Tim Trefren said as we pulled dusty saddles and sweaty blankets off our horses. Tim’s mount was a classy roan named Red. They called mine Propane Tank, both for his rotundity and for his habit of releasing an audible quantity of gas with nearly every step. “Up there” was a high ridge above the wall tents and lodgepole corral of Tim’s remote Wyoming hunting camp. We had just ridden down that steep ridge in the dark, our horses’ hooves throwing sparks every time their shoes nicked a rock in the trail. To me, in the dark atop a farting horse, the sparks looked like terrestrial versions of the shooting stars we had seen early that morning as we ascended the ridge, the Milky Way smeared across the sky.

The ridge is called the Greyback. Geologists would tell you it’s the upthrust portion of a subduction zone, vertical evidence of one of the continent’s growth plates. I’d guess it got its name because the miles-long hogback is punctuated by rocky heights that make it look like a giant’s backbone. And because it separates the Greys River watershed from that of the Hoback River to the east.

Whatever its derivation, the Greyback presides over gamey country in the Wyoming Range of western Wyoming. Tim, owner of Trefren Outfitters, and I had hunted elk since daybreak in the timberline basins that slide off the eastern side of the ridge. We had been in elk all day, and had seen moose, black bears, and even bighorn sheep on the distant red-rock slopes of Hoback Peak. Looking north from the highest points of the ridge, we could see the jagged crest of Grand Teton hovering above the town of Jackson like a snowy fang. We hadn’t gotten a shot at a bull, but soon after we mounted our horses for the long switchback ride down the ridge, we spotted a heavy-antlered animal crossing the trail in front of us. In the weak light of evening, it looked like a bull elk.

“That’s a helluva buck,” Tim whispered from the saddle, watching the mule deer disappear into the dark. “A helluva buck.”

Now, at the corrals, brushing down the horses and hanging saddles in the tack tent, Tim talked about the deer.

“We used to see bucks like that pretty regularly, back in the ’50s and ’60s,” Tim said. “Some hunters called them mossbacks, but most around here called them greybacks. They were just bigger—maybe 50 percent larger in body size than your typical mule deer. And their antlers… Well, there were some mighty fine racks that came out of that country back there.” Tim waved his curry brush back up toward the ridge.

I knew some of that history. The one-time world-record mule deer hailed from the Hoback. Back in the 1920s, a hunter killed the wide-racked buck for meat and left the skull behind. The antlers were picked up and found their way to a succession of bars, ending up at the Jackson Hole Museum, where you can still admire their dimensions: 217 inches of bone, enough to remain in the record book as the third-largest typical mule deer buck of all time.

“This was all horse country back then,” Tim continued. “If you wanted to hunt the Hoback, you had to plan to spend a week on your horse. Then the Jeeps started stabbing in, and the trails turned into roads. A guy in a chained-up Willy could hunt the Hoback in a couple days. Those big deer started getting harder and harder to find, to the point I’d almost say they’re extinct.”

Tim bucked his saddle on to its rack in the tack tent and spilled oats out of a Folgers can for the horses.

“Be something to turn up one of them greybacks.”

That was six years ago, but I never forgot about that buck. I didn’t shoot a Hoback bull with Tim, but later that season I killed a cow in the company of Tim’s son, also named Tim and called Junior around camp. In that season and over the next couple, I got to know the Trefrens and their main guide, Greg Kriese, like extended family. Tim Jr. kept inviting me to hunt with him, and I kept going—sometimes by myself, sometimes with friends—with a nonresident deer tag when I could draw one, with an elk tag when I couldn’t. Usually they gave me Propane Tank to ride.

My friendship with the clan grew so strong that I felt the blow when Tim Jr. called with the news. “Dad died last night. Funeral is in Thayne on Saturday. It would mean a lot to all of us if you could make it.”

I can’t recall the obligation that kept me away from Thayne that day, but I still feel guilty that I wasn’t there to send off Tim Sr., his empty saddle cinched on Red, his body in a horse-drawn hearse driven down Main Street by his son.

I also can’t recall what kept me from hunting with Tim Jr. and Greg that year, but I was determined to return to the Wyoming Range last fall. I had a preference point for a deer tag and had set aside a week in September for the Region H buck season. Then my friend Mike Stock called with a proposition. Mike is the centerfire ammunition product manager for Winchester, which has a longtime partnership with Browning. He had advised Browning on the development of a new line of ammunition. The iconic Buckmark would be imprinted on the cartridges’ headstamps. Mike is also one of my favorite hunting partners, and we try to get out in the field together at least once every season.

Let’s go deer hunting, Mike said, and be the first hunters to use Browning’s new Buckmark ammo in the field. Where should we go?

The answer leapt from my lips: The Wyoming Range.

That’s the abbreviated story of how Mike and I found ourselves pulling into the Trefrens’ wall-tent camp in late September, Browning rifles and ammo ready to go to work atop the Greyback. As I drove into camp, sun sifting through the lodgepole pine needles and little grey squirrels sprinting across the road, I felt a little like I was coming home. I wondered which horse I’d get dealt this year.

Mike hadn’t been a hard sell on Wyoming. There are other great places to hunt big mule deer—southern Utah, Colorado’s Western Slope, Arizona’s Kaibab Plateau, Oregon’s Blue Mountains, southeastern Idaho—but few with the history of the Wyoming Range.

I told Mike about my own background with the place—not only the monster buck I had spied with Tim Sr., but even before that, the pictures of heavy-racked, non-typical Greys River deer I had drooled over as a young Western hunter obsessed with big mule deer.

The Wyoming Range is legendary among trophy mule deer hunters. Maybe it’s the reputation of the Hoback Buck, but for years the range was known for its high-­country muleys—tall, heavy, non-typical bucks that summered in the subalpine basins of wildflowers and jack pine and wintered in the sagebrush desert that stretches east toward the Wind River Range.

Then word started trading among deer hunters that the Wyoming Range’s reputation was slipping. The state is issuing too many hunting tags, said some. It’s the drought, said others. But there was one undeniable consistency: Too many deer were dying out on the winter range.

Over the past couple of decades, much of that high-basin sagebrush has been impaired by gas wells, service roads, and power lines. When habitat becomes fractured, long, hard winters can be catastrophic for mule deer, especially when they follow droughty summers that leave the animals in poor physical condition. Trophy mule deer need five or six years to reach maturity, and tough winters come around about once a decade. The math suggests that weather and winter-range energy production may have as much impact on the Wyoming Range’s mossbacks as Jeeps had.

After I explained this dynamic to Mike, I could tell he was deflated. We were here to hunt big mule deer, but I made it sound like he should shoot the first forkhorn he saw.

“Relax,” I said as we settled into our canvas wall tent. “If any folks know big deer, it’s Junior and Greg.” But silently, I was worried. I had hunted here for years and had never had a deer in my sights that I wanted to shoot.

The camp’s daily ritual isn’t for night owls. Up at 4 a.m., breakfast in the cook tent, then in saddles by 5 and on the Greyback trail a couple of hours before light. The idea is to be in the high basins by sunup, glassing with binoculars for deer moving to their day beds. My horse this year: Hoback. Mike’s: Dickhead. Matt Nager, our photographer, rode Ugly Betty. Junior had to attend to work in town, so Greg, astride Red Ryder, guided us.

On our first morning on the ridge, Greg spotted a heavy-racked 4-point moving across a bowl, and it seemed a cinch to circle around the back side of the basin and shoot him when he walked into view on a game trail just below us. Only, after we waited a couple of hours, the buck never showed.

It’s like that in these high parks. What appears from a distance to be a featureless meadow is cut with gullies and fissures deep enough to funnel a deer out of danger.

So we hiked back to our horses and rode south in the midday heat, planning to eat lunch at the head of a series of basins that Greg said might be productive. Lunch is a highlight of any hunt with the Trefrens. Two sandwiches with condiments, a couple bags of chips, candy bars and granola bars, little pudding cups. Fruit Jell-O. An assortment of hard candies. It’s any fourth-grader’s fantasy grab bag. And it was all mine, in the most handsome lunchroom a big-game hunter could imagine.

As I settled against a fir trunk with my lunch bag, Greg pointed toward a strip of stunted pine that ran 1,000 yards away, from the middle of the steep basin toward the rim. “Keep an eye on that cover,” he said. “I guarantee there’s game in there.”

The sun was hot and the sandwiches tranquilizing, and every 30 minutes or so, I roused myself out of a haze to glass the jack pines. In midafternoon, I heard Greg whisper from behind his spotting scope.

“I got something here.” An urgency in his voice made me sit up straight. He fiddled and focused the scope and let out a deep breath. “Holy hell. That’s a giant.” Just like that, my lunch lethargy was gone as Mike, Matt, and I fought for position behind the scope. I scrunched my eyes in the optic. The heat was throwing up a shimmer, so the animal bedded in the shade of the pines looked like a deer in a fever dream, swimming in and out of focus. But I could make out its blocky body, double throat patch, and tall antlers blonde as straw.

If you’ve ever seen a trophy animal at an impossible distance, then you know that two things happen. First, you can’t stop looking at him, sizing up his headgear and wondering just how you might actually kill him. Second, you get a little paralyzed. To sit there and stare is easy and without consequence. To actually make a move ruins the perfection of possibility. What if he sees us and bolts? Or what if we blow our stalk and run him out of the basin. Or what if he simply walks into the scrubby pines and out of our sight? For nearly an hour we admired him, shooting video on our cell phones through the spotter and debating his dimensions.

I knew we’d have to move to kill him. We were 925 yards away, with no way to get closer on a straight line. We’d have to drop off our little ridge, hike to the top of the basin, and either take a long shot from above or work down into the basin without busting him.

I led the way, moving with purpose, with the others behind me. Here was possibly the largest mule deer I had ever seen in the flesh, and he was alarmingly aware. As we had watched him for that hour, he had gotten up from his bed three times. Every time he bedded back down, he situated himself so that he could scan the rim of the basin. Watching him, I realized here was a deer who knew the source of danger—the horse trail at the top of the ridge—and he knew how to avoid it, by staying in cover all day. The only place to spot him was from our lunch perch.

To kill him, we’d have to do everything right, so I made sure my profile was hidden by the ridge, that I didn’t knock an errant rock down the slope, and that I had a plan.

That plan was to gain the rim of the bowl and then to range the buck. I reckoned we’d be about 600 yards out, a long shot with my .30/06 and 185-grain Browning bullets even if I wasn’t shooting at an extreme downhill angle. But maybe, just maybe, a solution would reveal itself from the rim.

By the time we climbed to the top and assessed the situation from the rim of the basin, the sun was sinking low in the west. Worse, the buck was obscured by a little finger of rocks we hadn’t factored in from below. If I was going to kill this deer, I was going to have to enter his world: the steep, stony heart of the bowl.

I’d have to go alone, leaving my crew behind at the top to watch the action. But I’d also need an assurance the deer was still in the pines. So Greg sent Mike back to the spot from where we had originally seen the buck. If he was still in sight, Mike would raise his arms like a football referee signaling a touchdown. If he wasn’t there, Mike would sweep his hands horizontally, as though signaling an incomplete pass.

I dropped my pack and binocular, stuffed extra shells in my pockets, and pulled leather gloves on my hands. I felt like an Olympic mogul skier, about to drop into the run, so steep and gnarly was the terrain in front of me.

I took a couple of steps downhill and immediately knocked loose a fist-sized rock. It tumbled, caught air, and then clattered down the bowl, sounding like a lawn chair thrown down a stairway. No deer would stand for a racket like that.

I took a couple more mincing steps on the slope, trying to keep my balance and retain my stealth. Another rock rolled. How would I ever get to that rise of rocks undetected? I steeled myself. I’d simply have to sprint and hope to intercept the deer. I started to stride, only it was a cartoon sprint, on a 60-degree slope, the ankle-turning cobble trying to spill me on my butt, and rocks careening into thin air. My beautiful high-country buck surely must be in Idaho by now.

Then something surreal and impossible happened. Mid-stride, hyper-aware of the cacophony I was causing, I heard a noise quite unlike clattering rock. It was sudden, shrieking, and sky-fillingly loud, and I immediately realized it would cover my noise. I pitched down the bowl, windmilling my arms, using my rifle as a counterweight to keep my feet, dead-set on making the outcrop.

I reached the rock just as the source of the noise—two fighter jets—screamed over the Greyback, low enough for me to see rivets in their wings. I have no idea whether their low-altitude run is a regular occurrence, only that their timing this evening was a godsend. Just as quickly as they’d arrived, they were gone, and the high-mountain silence returned. I peered over the rock, and there was the line of pines 200 yards below me. But there was no buck in sight. I glassed through my riflescope, hoping to see an antler or an ear. Nothing. I was losing light fast, and felt a little surge of panic. Was the buck gone?

I turned and looked back up at the rim at Greg. Four hundred yards above me, silhouetted by the glowing sky, I could see Greg’s sign, his hands high in the air. The buck was still there. I was stuck on my rock, unable to move without dislodging more scree. My only choice was to wait and hope the buck might rise from his bed while I still had enough light to shoot.

I laid my leather gloves on the rough granite, and then the forend of my .30/06 X-Bolt on the gloves. I could only wait, and fret about the failing light.

When I saw the deer, he was feeding uphill, most of his body obscured by pine branches, but I knew it was him by his blocky body and tallow-ivory antlers. With no clear shot, I had to wait excruciatingly long minutes, glassing through my riflescope, until he was clear of bullet-deflecting obstructions. He was quartering away at a distance I estimated at 260 yards, but my rest was literally rock-solid. In the echoey bowl, my rifle shot sounded louder than the jets.

I waited for Mike to reach my perch, and the two of us walked to the buck while Greg and Matt came with the packs. The deer had cartwheeled down the scree after the hit, and it was nearly dark when we reached him. Normally, I would have held his antlers first, but what took my breath away was his body size. He was as large as a spike bull, with immense hindquarters and a barrel chest. I was marveling at his physical dimensions when Mike started laughing. “He looks just like the Buckmark,” he said, and I noticed that he did: The deep forks and long tines of the antlers might pass, in this flimsy light at least, for the iconic logo of the bullet I had just used to kill him.

When Greg and Matt arrived, we took photos and then started taking apart the deer. Our backpacks weren’t stout enough to haul all the meat, and it would take too long to hike out of the basin for the horses. So we quartered the buck and draped meat across the boughs of subalpine fir trees. I tied an orange vest to a tree and then urinated all around the little grove. This is lion and bear country, and I hoped the scent might deter scavengers until we could return in the morning with a pack horse.

In the dark of a moonless night, the hike out of the basin was long and strenuous. We reached the horses at midnight. I can’t recall a more enjoyable ride than that one, my hands caked with deer blood, the only sounds the tick of horses’ hooves on rocks and the creak of tired leather. I’m pretty sure my smile could have been seen from the satellites that streaked overhead, little pinpoints of light arcing against the deep stars.

I had killed my biggest mule deer, in one of my favorite hunting grounds, with a group of close friends. I could almost hear Tim Sr. ahead of me on Red. “Be something to turn up one of them greybacks…”.

This story was originally published in the September 2016 issue of Outdoor Life.

Andrew McKean is Outdoor Life’s hunting and conservation editor, drilling into issues that affect wildlife, wildlands, and the people who care about them. He’s also OL’s optics editor, helping readers to make informed buying decisions.

#8366. First Ski Descent of Meru Central

Tiphaine Duperier and Boris Langenstein of France have notched another Himalayan first ski descent, this time down the southwest face of Meru Central (6,310m) in India’s Garhwal Himalaya. The skiers are still surprised by how lucky they were.

Duperier admitted they started the expedition with low expectations after several projects earlier in the fall all failed.

“Snow conditions had been unforgiving,” she wrote. “We figured there was only a 3-in-10 chance of skiing the southwest face of Meru.”

But when they got there, the mountain was, they added, “generous” with them.

The three-peaked Meru massif, located in the Gangotri Glacier region of the Garhwal Himalaya, lies between Shivling and Thalay Sagar. It has three peaks: 6,660m Meru South, 6,310m Meru Central, and 6,450m Meru North. The ski descent line is in purple. Photo: Duperier/Langenstein

“We spent six days of reconnaissance and three [days] climbing the peak, [thanks to] an unprecedented stroke of luck in finding a way through the icefall and perfect snow in the upper section,” she explained.

The icefall on Meru Central. Photo: Boris Langenstein

The icefall at the base of the peak was indeed one of the most complex passages. The pair climbed a 15m pitch of WI4 and left a safety rope, which they also used to rappel down after the ski descent, Duperier told PlanetMountain.

Otherwise, the pair of regular expedition and skiing partners climbed alpine-style and pretty fast, reaching the summit in less than eight hours. According to their research, they completed the second-ever ascent of the southwest face of Meru, after an Indian team in 2023.

At the summit on Meru Central. Photo: Duperier/Langenstein

The skiers estimate they covered 1,500m on their descent, with some sections reaching 50 °. Snow conditions were good overall, hard but with a good grip.

“We skied like little monkeys on the wires in Rishikesh,” Duperier posted on social media. “It was just incredible, truly beautiful!”

While the climbers rappelled down the icefall onto the glacier below, the ski descent itself had no rappels or interruptions.

Duperier barely had time to return home to France to pick up a Piolet d’Or for the first alpine-style ascent of the Schell Route on the Rupal Face of Nanga Parbat, followed by the first ski descent from the 8,125m summit.

Tiphaine Duperier at the Piolets d’Or ceremony. Photo: Piotr Drozdz

#8365. From Day Hiker to Backpacker: My First Thru-Hike on the Trans-Catalina Trail

I’ve always lived with a chip on my shoulder.

I’ve always been on the short side, always first in line when elementary school teachers would determine line-up order by height. We were poor growing up — Section 8 kind of poor — living in the suburbs east of Los Angeles. My father died when I was two and my younger brother just six weeks old. My mother put herself through nursing school after his death, but she instilled in us at a young age: we would have to work hard, very hard, for the things we wanted in life.

Because of this chip on my shoulder — chips, really — I’ve lived my entire life fueled by the fact I had things to prove to the world. As a young, short, poor, fatherless girl, that fire was lit under my ass at a very young age and it hasn’t gone out.

I tell you all this to not tease out sympathy for me, but rather to give you an understanding of who I am, where I came from and my reasons for getting into backpacking. To put it simply, backpacking is hard, long, grueling and can often be unforgiving. I want to see how I can measure up against it.

But putting things simply isn’t why I’m here, nor is it why you’re here reading this blog, amongst the many other blogs. So we’ll call this is a preface.

My name is Bria Manning, and I’m a 30-year-old sports multimedia producer living in rural southwest Montana. That’s me now. Before that, though, I was a California girl, born and raised in the suburbs of Los Angeles by my mother, a registered nurse. I’m the middle child with an older sister and younger brother. Though I was the most difficult for my mother to raise, if you were to ask her now who her favorite child is, she, like any good mother, would respond, “I love all my children equally for different reasons.” But I call BS. I know deep down it’s me.

For as long as I can remember I’ve had The Itch: to leave, to adventure, to romp and explore. As a kid, I wrote semifictional short stories about my life. In them, I drove a black Chevrolet Avalanche — the same truck my crush’s mother drove — and I would take off on the road whenever The Itch compelled me to. Now that I’m a grown up, that hasn’t changed; I’m merely living my teenage fantasy dreams out. My entire life, I’ve loved my freedom more than anything.

In Southern California, The Itch pulled me out towards the neighboring hills of Whittier. The hills hugged the community so tightly, and there was never a shortage of trails for me to explore. In high school, I’d ride my bike to the trailhead in those hills, lock it up and then continue on foot. I liked the solace of the dusty trails and the fact there was an entire network of them so I could go down any path I wanted. I loved exploring different routes, taking in different scenery, trying for a more challenging elevation profile on certain days long before I could even tell you what an elevation profile was.

As I grew older, my love for hiking also grew. I began planning road trips around day hikes — to Big Bear, to the Sierra, to Bryce Canyon, to Las Vegas, to Sedona. I had — have — a group of friends who equally loved the outdoors, and my 20’s were defined by these trips around California and the Southwest to bear witness to natural beauty and escape the bustle of metropolitan life.

For all my excursions, though, and for all my love of the outdoors and adventures and even for The Itch to which I so willingly and often submitted to, I was always a day hiker. I in fact did not go on my first backpacking trip until this past summer, after nearly two years of living in Montana.

Backpacking was something I’d always wanted to get into. My sister, her husband and their friends spent nearly every summer backpacking in the Sierra in their 20’s and 30’s. Every year, I’d tell myself, “Next year. Next year I’ll go with them.” But things always got in the way — undergrad, then COVID, then grad school, then a career. After I moved to Montana to be with my boyfriend (now fiance) Kade, I was looking 30 straight in the face.

My move to Montana is what also brought me to Jessica “Stitches” Guo. In 2025, she became the first known woman to link the Continental Divide Trail and Great Divide Trail in a calendar year. My Instagram algorithm brought her journey to my attention.

At the time, I was working as the sports editor of a local Montana newspaper. It was the summer, a slow time for sports desk. I thought meeting up with her as she came through Anaconda would be the perfect opportunity to profile her for our newspaper. As it turned out, it became so much more for me.

I met Guo at a local market and followed her around as she did her town chores. I was so curious as to what a resupply looked like on a trek such as this, what sort of food thru-hikers ate. I drove Guo to the hiker hut in town and conducted my interview with her there, learning all about her life — how she’d come to want to link the CDT and GDT, how she had hiked the Pacific Crest Trail already too.

But I was most curious about how she’d begun. So often, we join an influencer or content creator’s journey online while they’re in the midst of it, whether it’s their first one or their third one or their tenth. As someone who’d always had an interest in backpacking but was also intimidated about where to start, I wanted to pick Guo’s brain about how and why she had gotten started.

I asked her if there was one determining factor that led her to her decision to hike the PCT.

“I felt like, if I didn’t do it then, that I was never going to do it,” Guo told me. “Like I feel sometimes you realize that time just keeps going by and by and by. You can say, ‘Okay, next year, next year, next year,’ just keep putting that up. You’ll be 70 and you’ll be like, ‘Oh, you know what? I wanted to hike this trail.’ And life only gets busier. I think if you have a goal, I think you should first go do it.”

I went home that evening and told Kade about my conversation with Guo. He knew I’ve always had an interest in backpacking.

That’s when I channeled my inner Stitches and I told myself and Kade, “No, not ‘next year’ or the year after that. Actually next year.”

Settling on the Trans-Catalina Trail was an easy, simple decision for me. I’d had my eye on it my whole adult life, having been born and raised in Southern California. I’m even sure that, while on a fifth-grade GATE field trip to Catalina Island, the trails we had hiked were on the Trans-Catalina Trail. Even then I remember how brutally hot and exposed the trail was, and I was struck by the power lines that looped around even in the island’s rugged interior.

It seemed like the ideal first multi-day backpacking trip: just about 40 miles over four days, with very established campgrounds with potable water. No wildlife to be wary of save the buffalo, but coming from grizzly country I wasn’t too concerned. The elevation profile, while daunting at nearly 10,000 feet of gain overall, should be challenging but nothing I couldn’t handle, especially coming from living at over 5,000 feet of altitude.

I’ll save specifics for how I trained for this hike for another blog, but I will say that it was just a little over a year ago that I promised myself I would hike the Trans-Catalina Trail in 2026 for my first thru-hike. I wanted to do something big and special for myself for my 30th birthday, but early October is still much too hot in Southern California. Spring was an option, but that would leave me just a couple months to train for it — and it would be limited to just the gym, because while I’m acclimated to Montana climate, there is still no way in hell I’m doing a winter backpacking trip to prepare.

So that left the fall. Thanksgiving week seemed the safest option; it’s still quite warm in Southern California on Thanksgiving but never extremely hot. Plus, Kade decided he would come with me for this first experience. As a business owner in small-town Montana, using the Thanksgiving holiday to hike would be the most doable option for him. That gave us the entire spring, summer and early fall to get us into backpacking shape.

I awoke early on January 1 of this year very differently than I had in the New Year’s Days of past. No hangover, not even very sleepy — Kade and I had retired early, like responsible, boring adults.

While Kade lingered in bed with our dogs, Roxy and Gigi, I got up and set my laptop down on the dining room table. I had spent the past couple months diving into all the research into the Trans-Catalina Trail. One of the things I’ve grown to love most about backpacking training is the research — spending hours zooming in and out and around on onX Backcountry, studying the trails and terrain; reading about the history of the area I’ll be exploring; watching countless YouTube videos of hikers’ journeys. In the year leading up to this trip, which in exactly a week of this writing I’ll be embarking upon, I have already saved handfuls of shorter thru-hikes and backpacking routes on All Trails for Kade and I to do next summer. That’s another facet of this backpacking journey I’ve grown to love: it gives you a tangible goal to work towards.

By the time it was January 1 and permits and campgrounds reservations for the Trans-Catalina Trail had opened up on the Catalina Island Conservancy’s website, I knew exactly which campgrounds and sites I wanted. A year early, and I had our itinerary down. I had logged each day by mileage and elevation gain and executed a game plan based on my research. Kade, not much of a planner, was happy to stand back and let me plan and research away.

About 20 minutes later — and a couple hundred dollars less in my bank account, as the campsites for two people on Catalina are quite hefty — and we were all booked to hike the Trans-Catalina Trail from November 24 to November 27. Now it was time to spend the year preparing for it, to see if this is something I could actually do.

#8364. This Traditional Archer Tagged a Big 8-Pointer With a Longbow and Stone Point Arrowhead He Made Himself

Published Nov 9, 2026 2:20 PM EST

Get everything from whitetail news and opinion pieces, to advanced hunting tactics and cutting-edge gear reviews.

It was the evening of October 25 when Joe McConnell, a traditional bowhunter from central Ohio, climbed into a ladder stand with a backdrop of heavy cover.

McConnell was hunting with a longbow in a narrow strip of woods that he owns. The spot was overlooking a travel lane deer were using to enter a large field of standing corn.

“I was really after a nice 10-point buck I had on trail cameras,” McConnell tells Outdoor Life. “The wind was perfect that evening, blowing right in my face. I was looking forward to filling my first landowner tag with a deer on my own property.”

“I’d made a mock scrape in front of my stand, with a licking branch above it about 12 yards from my ladder,” says the 38-year-old archer. “I heard him in the corn about six rows in, and he came to check the scrape.

“I saw his rack above the standing corn field coming to me, and when he stopped broadside quartering away at 12 yards, I took my shot.”

The buck was not the 10-point he was after. Instead, it was a dandy 8-pointer that McConnell couldn’t pass up.

McConnell drew his 64-inch, 55-pound longbow he’d made from an Osage orange tree limb. Then, shooting instinctively, he released a 26-inch arrow he’d made of cane and fletched with white turkey feathers.

His arrow hit the buck perfectly behind the shoulder, the super-sharp stone broadhead he handmade drove deep into the deer’s chest.

“I saw him race and tear through the corn field,” says McConnell, who owns a hardwood flooring and restoration business. “I heard him crashing away through corn stalks, and then nothing.”

The bowman found a good blood trail where the buck stood, and the trail was easy to follow through the corn.

“He only went about 75 yards before falling dead,” he says. “My stone broadhead did an incredible job, driving through its liver, a lung, and smashing into a rib on the opposite side of the buck. The arrow point hit bone and stopped or it would have completely gone through the buck’s hide on the opposite side.

“Everything really came together for me with that deer. I’ve taken lots of animals with the bows and arrows I’ve made. But it’s the first deer I’ve taken with a stone broadhead that I knapped myself – and it was devastating.”

McConnell has taken plenty of deer and wild hogs with traditional archery gear he’s made. He also shot a buffalo with his traditional equipment, and a stone point head he’d made specifically for the hunt.

He called some friends who helped get his big 8-point buck out of the field. The field-dressed buck weighed 180 pounds at the processor. It had an estimated live weight of well over 200 pounds.

He will eventually have the deer scored via Buckmasters, and his taxidermist estimated the rack to be about 140 inches.

Read Next: Killing a Grizzly the Old-Fashioned Way: With a Longbow and a Stone-Point Arrowhead

McConnell models his canted bow shooting style after legendary archer Howard Hill. He leans forward when drawing his bow, anchors his arrow at the corner of his mouth, and uses his bare hand holding his bow as an arrow rest.

“I got started in archery when I was only 14,” McConnell says. “It’s been a lot of fun learning about making bows, arrows, and now stone broadheads. Traditional equipment is remarkably efficient bowhunting gear.”

Bob McNally has been an outdoor writer since shortly after the earth’s crust cooled. He has written 12 outdoor books, more than 5,000 outdoor magazine stories (including many for Outdoor Life) and more newspaper outdoor columns and features than there are hairs on a grizzly bear.

#8361. Arctic Town Kills Dozens of Grizzlies Feeding on Dump

For years, the grizzlies near Inuvik in Canada’s western Arctic relied on a stable source of food — the town dump. Generations of bears grew up feeding there. In 2025, wildlife officials found that over 40 grizzlies regularly visited the dump.

In 2025, before the fence was built, trail cameras captured multiple grizzlies hanging around the dump, looking for food. Photo: Government of the Northwest Territories

It was too much. This year, the town built an electric fence around the site, hoping the bears would move on. They didn’t. Some started coming into town looking for food. Others just hung around the fence, searching for a way in.

“They would just do these laps around the dump, and they would just be emaciated, sickly,” said Toby Halle, a Renewable Resources officer based in Inuvik, told the CBC. “They don’t know what to do with themselves. And quite frankly, we don’t know what to do with them.”

Inuvik, population about 3,500, was the first community in that part of the Arctic to try to wean the bears off their dependence on dump food with such a fence, which cost about $700,000. The problem was, the bears had not learned to depend on any other source of food.

“We’ve probably had three to four generations of bears that have been using that landfill,” said local mayor Peter Clarkson. In the end, the town took a drastic solution — but one that was probably unavoidable in the circumstances: They shot 28 bears.

Tragic though this is, officials hope that within the next couple of years, the remaining bears in the area will move on and learn to eat more natural fare.

Many other Arctic towns still have open dumps where bears come to feed. Photo: Government of the Northwest Territories
